patient.name: Margaret O'Connell
patient.complaint: Shaky hands for 3 years, now spilling tea and struggling to write
background: Mild asthma: salbutamol inhaler as needed
Her mother and brother both 'had a shake'
Drinks 4 cups of coffee a day
Retired primary school teacher in Ealing

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a bilateral action or postural tremor, a family history and relief with alcohol; Parkinson's disease (resting, asymmetric, bradykinesia) is the key distractor.

points: Margaret, 64: both hands shake for 3 years.
Mother and brother had the same shake.

steps.lead: A **postural and action** tremor of both hands, with no parkinsonism, is the definition of essential tremor.
Margaret's mother and brother fit **autosomal dominant** inheritance.

points: Arms outstretched: fine, fast tremor appears in both hands.
Finger-nose: tremor persists through the movement.
Voice slightly shaky; mild 'no-no' head tremor.

steps.lead: Bilateral tremor, **worse with arms outstretched**, with head titubation and voice tremor, and a normal tone and speed of movement.

visual.title: Tremor frequency

steps.q: Which feature most supports essential tremor over Parkinson's disease?
steps.r: ET is a **postural/action** tremor. Rest tremor, asymmetry and bradykinesia point to Parkinson's.

visual.title: Margaret's tremor through the day
visual.caption: Worse after caffeine, briefly better after alcohol.

steps.lead: Margaret's tremor is worse after **coffee** and settles after a glass of wine: a strong clinical clue.

steps.text: Alcohol relief is a **diagnostic clue**, not a treatment. Never advise drinking to control the tremor.

steps.lead: It is benign, but Margaret is spilling drinks and cannot write: **functional impairment** is the main complication.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' where the answer is clinical diagnosis, or TFTs if the stem hints at another cause.

steps.r: Essential tremor is a **clinical diagnosis**. DaTscan is only for doubt about parkinsonism.

steps.lead: Margaret's history and examination make the diagnosis; no scan is needed.

steps.title: Bloods to exclude other causes
steps.text: Normal thyroid function: no hyperthyroid tremor.

steps.text: Other causes of an action tremor to think of: **hyperthyroidism**, drugs (salbutamol, lithium, valproate), caffeine and alcohol withdrawal.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?' where propranolol is the answer, unless the stem mentions asthma (then primidone); deep brain stimulation for severe refractory cases.

points: Margaret wants treatment: the tremor stops her writing.
She has **asthma** and uses salbutamol most weeks.

steps.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line drug for Margaret?
steps.r: Propranolol is first-line for ET, but it is **contraindicated in asthma**, so **primidone** is used.

steps.lead: Without asthma Margaret would get **propranolol**; her asthma makes **primidone** the right choice.

steps.text: **Levodopa** is for Parkinson's disease, not essential tremor.

steps.lead: If primidone fails, Margaret could try **topiramate, gabapentin or clonazepam**.

visual.title: Margaret's response to primidone
visual.caption: Partial improvement: she can write and drink again.

steps.lead: If her tremor became severe and drug-resistant, **deep brain stimulation** would be considered.
Margaret's plan follows **NICE CKS on tremor**.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why ET is an action rather than a rest tremor, why alcohol helps, how propranolol works and the mode of inheritance.

steps.lead: Margaret's tremor is thought to come from abnormal oscillation in the **cerebello-thalamo-cortical** loop.

steps.title: The tremor loop
nodes: Rhythmic tremor during posture and action

steps.lead: Margaret's hands are still at rest because the faulty circuit controls **posture and voluntary movement**, not resting tone (the basal ganglia in Parkinson's).

steps.q: Why does a glass of wine briefly settle Margaret's tremor?
o: It treats an underlying thyroid problem
steps.r: Alcohol suppresses the abnormal **cerebellar/olivary** oscillation; the effect is short-lived.

steps.lead: The relief from wine is brief, so it is a **clue, not a treatment**.
Propranolol blocks **beta-adrenergic** amplification of tremor; that is also why it is unsafe with Margaret's asthma (beta-2 blockade causes bronchospasm).

glossary.essential tremor: A benign, often inherited postural and action tremor without parkinsonian features.
glossary.postural tremor: Tremor present when holding a position against gravity, such as arms outstretched.
glossary.action tremor: Tremor during voluntary movement, such as pouring or writing.
glossary.resting tremor: Tremor when the limb is relaxed and supported, typical of Parkinson's disease.
glossary.intention tremor: Tremor that worsens approaching a target, typical of cerebellar disease.
glossary.pill-rolling: Thumb-and-finger rest tremor of Parkinson's disease.
glossary.titubation: Rhythmic nodding ('yes-yes') or shaking ('no-no') tremor of the head.
glossary.parkinsonism: Bradykinesia with rigidity, rest tremor or postural instability.
glossary.bradykinesia: Slowness of movement with decreasing amplitude on repetition.
glossary.rigidity: Increased tone throughout the range of movement, not velocity-dependent.
glossary.cogwheel rigidity: Rigidity with superimposed tremor giving a ratchety feel, typical of Parkinson's.
glossary.autosomal dominant: Inheritance where one copy of the gene causes the condition; each child has a 50% risk.
glossary.Hz: Hertz: cycles per second, used to describe tremor frequency.
glossary.propranolol: Non-selective beta-blocker; first-line treatment for essential tremor.
glossary.primidone: Anticonvulsant used for essential tremor when propranolol is unsuitable.
glossary.topiramate: Anticonvulsant used as a further option for essential tremor.
glossary.gabapentin: Anticonvulsant sometimes used for essential tremor.
glossary.deep brain stimulation: Implanted electrodes stimulating the thalamus to suppress severe tremor.
glossary.beta-adrenergic: Relating to beta receptors stimulated by adrenaline and noradrenaline.
glossary.bronchospasm: Narrowing of the airways; a risk of non-selective beta-blockers in asthma.
glossary.cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuit: Loop from cerebellum through thalamus to motor cortex, thought to generate essential tremor.
glossary.inferior olive: Brainstem nucleus linked to the cerebellum, thought to drive tremor oscillation.
glossary.basal ganglia: Deep brain nuclei controlling movement initiation, damaged in Parkinson's disease.
glossary.DaTscan: Dopamine transporter scan that distinguishes Parkinson's disease from essential tremor when in doubt.
glossary.TFTs: Thyroid function tests: TSH and free T4.
glossary.hyperthyroidism: Overactive thyroid causing a fine tremor, weight loss and palpitations.
glossary.enhanced physiological tremor: Exaggerated normal tremor from caffeine, anxiety, thyroid disease or drugs such as salbutamol.
glossary.levodopa: Dopamine precursor used in Parkinson's disease, not essential tremor.
glossary.NICE CKS: NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries, practical primary care guidance.

technique.stem: A 59 year old man has a 4 year history of shaking of both hands. It is worst when he holds a cup or writes. His father had a similar tremor. The tremor is less noticeable after a pint of beer. On examination there is a fine tremor with arms outstretched and normal tone. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about tremor: decide rest vs action first.

clues: less noticeable after a pint of beer
steps.x: Bilateral action/postural tremor, family history, alcohol relief, normal tone.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Cerebellar tremor is intentional, with ataxia and nystagmus.
Pulse normal and long, inherited history.
PD gives a rest tremor, asymmetry and bradykinesia; tone is normal.

steps.x: **C. Essential tremor.** Rule: bilateral action tremor + family history + alcohol relief = essential tremor.

technique.stem: A 52 year old woman has a 2 year history of a bilateral postural hand tremor. Her mother had a similar tremor. She has no weight loss, palpitations or heat intolerance. Examination shows normal tone and speed of movement.

normal tone and speed of movement
steps.x: Typical ET with no thyroid features and no parkinsonism.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Only if parkinsonism is uncertain; it is not.

steps.x: **E. No investigation: clinical diagnosis.** Rule: typical ET needs no scan; TFTs only if a thyroid cause is possible.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

technique.stem: A 34 year old man has a bilateral action tremor of both hands. His father, his paternal grandmother and his sister are similarly affected. His mother and brother are not.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mode of inheritance?

steps.x: Mode of inheritance: draw the pedigree.

clues: father, his paternal grandmother and his sister
His mother and brother are not
steps.x: Every generation affected, both sexes, and father-to-son transmission.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Autosomal dominant**, as expected for essential tremor.

elim: Would usually skip generations, with unaffected parents.
Passed only through the mother; here it comes via the father.
He inherited it from his father: male-to-male transmission excludes X-linked inheritance.
Father-to-son transmission and an affected sister exclude it.

steps.x: **A. Autosomal dominant.** Rule: ET is typically autosomal dominant.

practice.stem: A 62 year old man has a 5 year history of tremor of both hands, worse when pouring tea. His brother has the same problem. On examination, the tremor appears when his arms are outstretched. Tone and gait are normal. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A bilateral postural and action tremor with a family history and normal tone is essential tremor. Parkinson's gives a rest tremor with rigidity and bradykinesia.

steps.x: Bilateral postural/action tremor with family history and no parkinsonism.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: No intention tremor, ataxia or nystagmus.
Rest tremor, asymmetry and rigidity are absent.

steps.x: **B. Essential tremor.** Bilateral + action + family history = ET.

practice.stem: A 70 year old woman has a shaky head that moves side to side ('no-no') and a tremulous voice. Her hands shake when she holds a newspaper. Her hands are still when resting in her lap. There is no rigidity or bradykinesia. Her pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 140/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Head titubation and voice tremor with a postural hand tremor and no parkinsonism are classic essential tremor.

steps.x: Titubation, voice tremor, postural hand tremor, no rest tremor.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Gives a sustained abnormal head posture, not just tremor.
Chorea and cognitive change, not tremor.
Head tremor is uncommon; rest tremor and bradykinesia are absent.
Young patients with liver disease and a wing-beating tremor.

steps.x: **B. Essential tremor.** Head titubation + voice tremor = ET until proven otherwise.

practice.stem: A 55 year old man with essential tremor starts propranolol and his tremor improves. He asks how the tablet works. His pulse rate falls from 82 bpm to 64 bpm.

steps.x: It **blocks beta-adrenergic enhancement** of the tremor.
**A. Blocks beta-adrenergic enhancement of tremor.** Propranolol = peripheral beta blockade.
